subject: Chemistry

uncertain: coordinating hybrid orbitals with sigma/pi overlap
distinguishing electron-domain geometry from molecular shape

hardest_target.rationale: The preset marks sigma/pi-to-hybrid coordination uncertain. These items require preserving Lewis/domain meaning while allocating sigma hybrids and unhybridised p orbitals without double-counting, and Q3 adds plane/perpendicular translation.
hardest_target.interaction: Cumulative staged SVG: sigma-domain frame -> leftover p orbital(s) -> side-on pi overlap -> orbital-job closure check.
hardest_target.uncertainty: No learner attempt data exist; this is a learner-relative authoring hypothesis, not measured mastery.

missing_matrix_cells_note: This ten-item brief does not cover the full 28-cell matrix; no labels were inflated to fill missing cells.

items.verified_answer: BF3 is treated by the introductory localized model as three electron domains at B: sp2 with trigonal-planar bonded-atom arrangement. NH3 has four electron domains at N because its lone pair is an additional domain: sp3, tetrahedral electron-domain geometry and trigonal-pyramidal molecular shape. Therefore three sigma bonds alone are insufficient.
items.X: Whether the central count is only sigma bonds or the full set of electron domains, including lone pairs.
items.Y: The preset says simple Lewis structures and central electron-domain counting are demonstrated.
items.Z: Count all local electron domains first, then connect 3 domains to the introductory sp2 model and 4 domains to sp3 while separating electron-domain geometry from molecular shape.
items.W: Explain why the lone-pair domain changes the model/shape conclusion even though both centres have three sigma bonds.
hints: Do not stop at the number of sigma bonds; ask what else occupies a direction around the central atom.
Compare the total number of local electron domains at B and N, counting the nitrogen lone pair.
Use the demonstrated 3-domain versus 4-domain geometry rule, but leave the final comparison and shape statement to your own response.

representation.reason: A paired domain/shape schematic can make the extra lone-pair domain visible without writing the final hybrid labels.

misconception.M1: Three sigma bonds automatically mean three electron domains and therefore sp2.
misconception.M2: Ask the learner to count central domains in BF3 and NH3 before naming any hybridisation.
misconception.M3: Count bonding directions and lone-pair regions as electron domains; molecular shape then omits lone-pair positions from the atom arrangement.

items.independent_check: Recount domains directly from the Lewis descriptions: BF3 = 3, NH3 = 4; the conclusions must differ.

items.verified_answer: Carbon in H2C=O has three electron domains and is described as sp2 in the introductory localized model. The C=O double bond contains one sigma and one pi component. Three sp2 hybrids support the sigma framework; one unhybridised carbon 2p orbital remains for the pi overlap. The C=O multiple bond is one electron domain even though it contains two shared electron pairs.
items.X: What must stay invariant when translating from Lewis-domain counting to an orbital account of the C=O double bond.
items.Y: The learner has demonstrated Lewis structures and domain counting, including the rule that a multiple bond occupies one direction/domain.
items.Z: Map three carbon domains to three sp2 sigma-framework directions, then allocate the remaining carbon p orbital to the pi component.
items.W: Keep the one-domain C=O direction distinct from its one-sigma-plus-one-pi bond composition without double-counting.
hints: Count directions of electron density around carbon, not the number of shared pairs in the double bond.
A three-domain carbon uses three in-plane sigma-framework directions in the introductory sp2 description.
After those three directions are assigned, identify which unhybridised carbon orbital can overlap side-on; do not count it as a fourth domain.

representation.reason: The hardest distinction is representational: three in-plane sigma directions plus a perpendicular unhybridised p orbital.

misconception.M1: The C=O double bond contributes two electron domains because it contains two shared pairs.
misconception.M2: Ask whether replacing C=O by two separate C–O single bonds would preserve the same number of directions around carbon.
misconception.M3: Domain counting tracks directions/regions; sigma/pi decomposition tracks bond components. Keep those ledgers separate.

items.independent_check: Three carbon domains account for two C-H directions plus the C=O direction; the double bond still decomposes independently into 1 sigma + 1 pi.

items.verified_answer: Each ethene carbon is described as sp2. Three sp2 hybrid directions at each carbon lie in the molecular plane and form the sigma framework (C–H and the C–C sigma bond). One unhybridised p orbital remains on each carbon perpendicular to that plane; the two parallel p orbitals overlap side-on above and below the plane to form the pi component.
items.X: Which geometric/orbital features of the Lewis structure must be preserved in an orbital-overlap diagram.
items.Y: The learner can count three domains at each carbon; the authored bridge is that sp2 supplies three coplanar hybrids and leaves one perpendicular p orbital.
items.Z: Place the sigma framework in the molecular plane and then add the two parallel unhybridised p orbitals perpendicular to it for side-on overlap.
items.W: Complete the plane-versus-perpendicular correspondence and show the p–p side-on overlap without using the same orbital for both sigma and pi jobs.
hints: First draw only the nuclei and sigma-bond directions; decide what belongs to the molecular plane.
At each carbon, three sp2 directions belong to the sigma framework, leaving one unhybridised p orbital.
Add the remaining p orbitals perpendicular to the plane and parallel to each other; leave the final overlap annotation for your attempt.

representation.reason: A staged orbital diagram is essential to the translation demand and supports a non-answer-bearing plane/perpendicular construction.

misconception.M1: Use an sp2 hybrid orbital itself for the pi bond, or place the unhybridised p orbitals in the molecular plane.
misconception.M2: Ask the learner to mark which carbon orbitals have already been consumed by sigma bonding before drawing pi overlap.
misconception.M3: Allocate orbital jobs once: sp2 hybrids form the sigma framework; the remaining unhybridised p orbitals form the pi component by side-on overlap.

items.independent_check: Every carbon has exactly three sp2 sigma directions plus one unhybridised p orbital; the two p orbitals are parallel and perpendicular to the molecular plane.

items.verified_answer: Central carbon in CO2 has two electron domains, so the introductory localized model uses sp hybridisation: two sp hybrids point 180° apart for the two sigma bonds. Two unhybridised carbon p orbitals remain, mutually perpendicular and both perpendicular to the molecular axis. Each C=O contains one sigma and one pi component, so the two double bonds give two sigma and two pi components while the nuclei remain linear.
items.X: How two Lewis electron domains, two sigma directions, and two independent pi components can all belong to one linear carbon centre.
items.Y: The demonstrated anchor is the two-domain linear rule; the authored orbital bridge is that sp uses one s + one p and leaves two p orbitals unhybridised.
items.Z: Coordinate the linear two-sp-hybrid sigma framework with two remaining perpendicular p orbitals, one for each pi component.
items.W: Make the ordering/bridge that reconciles two electron domains with two sigma plus two pi components without treating each pi component as a new domain.
hints: Start from the central-carbon domain count: each C=O multiple bond points in one direction and counts as one domain.
A two-domain introductory model uses two opposite sigma-framework directions and leaves two carbon p orbitals unused by that framework.
Those two remaining p orbitals can support two independent side-on overlaps; keep the molecular axis linear while you complete the sigma/pi inventory.

representation.reason: The learner must coordinate a linear axis with two mutually perpendicular p-orbital planes; prose alone makes double-counting likely.

misconception.M1: Four bond components around carbon imply four electron domains or sp3.
misconception.M2: Ask the learner to count directions in the Lewis structure separately from sigma/pi components in the bond ledger.
misconception.M3: A multiple bond is one domain direction; in the sp model two hybrids form sigma bonds and the two leftover p orbitals supply the two pi components.

items.independent_check: Orbital inventory at carbon is 2 sp hybrids + 2 unhybridised p orbitals = 4 valence orbitals; bond-component inventory is 2 sigma + 2 pi, while the domain count remains 2.

items.verified_answer: The observations do not support the claim. BF3 and NH3 each have three central sigma bonds, but NH3 also has a lone-pair domain. The decisive introductory warrant is total local electron-domain count, not sigma-bond count alone: for common small main-group localized examples, 2/3/4 domains are described as sp/sp2/sp3. BF3 is therefore the three-domain case, whereas NH3 is the four-domain case. Observed shape can motivate or test such a model, but shape alone is not direct proof that particular atomic orbitals literally hybridised.
items.X: Whether the examples license the universal claim and what evidence is allowed to determine the introductory hybrid label.
items.Y: The learner can count domains; authoritative background treats hybridisation as an orbital model used to rationalize bonding/geometry rather than a shape-only measurement.
items.Z: Use BF3/NH3 as a counterexample pair, state the domain-count warrant, and separate model assignment from direct experimental proof of orbital composition.
items.W: Reject the claim with the decisive lone-pair/domain warrant and state a bounded, defensible introductory rule.

misconception.M2: Ask what observation distinguishes BF3 and NH3 before allowing any hybrid label.
misconception.M3: Use explicit Lewis/domain evidence to choose the introductory model; treat geometry as model evidence, not direct orbital measurement.

items.independent_check: Apply the proposed rule to both BF3 and NH3; a rule based only on three sigma bonds cannot classify both consistently.

items.verified_answer: Carbon in CH3F has four local electron domains (four sigma bonds) and is described as sp3 in the introductory model, with approximately tetrahedral domain directions. Replacing one H by F changes the identity and therefore properties such as polarity and typically bond length/strength, but it does not change the number of directions/domains around carbon.
items.X: Which feature determines the count of local domain directions and which features may change when H is replaced by F.
items.Y: The learner has demonstrated four-domain geometry counting.
items.Z: Keep the four-direction domain count fixed while distinguishing it from bond-specific properties.
items.W: Explain why the introductory local hybridisation/domain geometry stays the same without claiming C–F and C–H bonds are otherwise identical.
hints: Count the directions of electron density around carbon before comparing atom identities.
CH4 and CH3F each give carbon four sigma-bond directions; ask what that preserves in the local domain model.
Now separate that preserved geometry from properties that depend on which atoms are bonded.

representation.reason: For this learner the decisive act is verbal distinction between domain count and bond-specific properties; an additional orbital drawing would be decorative.

misconception.M1: Changing H to F must change carbon hybridisation, or conversely identical hybridisation means C–F and C–H bonds have identical properties.
misconception.M2: Ask whether atom substitution changes the number of central bond directions before discussing polarity or bond strength.
misconception.M3: Hybridisation/domain geometry tracks the local directional model; bond properties also depend on the bonded atoms and are not fixed by that label alone.

items.independent_check: Both CH4 and CH3F have four central sigma-bond directions; the explanation must preserve that count while allowing bond-specific differences.

items.verified_answer: In HCN, carbon has two domains (H–C and C≡N) and nitrogen has two local domains (the C≡N direction and its lone pair), so both are described as sp in the introductory localized model. The C≡N triple bond contains one sigma and two pi components. Each atom uses sp hybrids for the axial sigma/lone-pair framework and retains two unhybridised p orbitals for the two mutually perpendicular pi overlaps.
items.X: How a triple bond can contain three bond components while counting as one domain at each bonded atom.
items.Y: The learner has the two-domain linear rule; the orbital bridge is that sp leaves two unhybridised p orbitals.
items.Z: Coordinate local domain counts at C and N with the one-sigma/two-pi decomposition of C≡N.
items.W: Explain compatibility without counting the two pi components as extra electron-domain directions.
hints: At each centre, count directions/regions first: a multiple bond occupies one direction.
A two-domain introductory model leaves two p orbitals unhybridised at each atom.
Use the axial hybrid direction for the sigma component and the two p pairs for side-on pi overlap; keep the domain ledger separate.

representation.reason: A linear-axis plus two perpendicular p-p overlap schematic directly supports the compatibility demanded by the item.

misconception.M1: A triple bond contributes three electron domains, forcing more than two local directions.
misconception.M2: Ask the learner to list domain directions and bond components in two separate columns.
misconception.M3: Count the C≡N connection once for local geometry, then decompose that one connection into one sigma plus two pi components for bonding.

items.independent_check: At both C and N the local domain count is 2, while the C≡N bond-component count is independently 1 sigma + 2 pi.

items.verified_answer: Both centres are described as sp3 in the introductory model because each has four electron domains. Carbon has four bonding domains and its bonded atoms occupy a tetrahedral arrangement. Nitrogen has three bonding domains plus one lone pair, so its electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral but its bonded atoms form a trigonal-pyramidal molecular shape. The same hybridisation label therefore does not require the same atom-only shape.
items.X: Why the same four-domain/hybrid label can coexist with different arrangements of bonded atoms.
items.Y: The learner knows four-domain tetrahedral electron-domain geometry; the uncertain bridge is electron-domain geometry versus molecular shape.
items.Z: Compare which of the four domain positions are occupied by bonded atoms versus a lone pair at C and N.
items.W: Explain same sp3 domain model but tetrahedral carbon atom arrangement versus trigonal-pyramidal nitrogen atom arrangement.
hints: Count all four domain positions at each centre before looking only at atoms.
At carbon all four positions are bonds; at nitrogen one position is a lone pair.
Molecular shape names atom positions, not every electron-domain position; use that distinction to finish the comparison.

representation.reason: A shared tetrahedral-domain scaffold with bond/lone-pair occupancy makes the geometry-versus-shape distinction visible.

misconception.M1: The label sp3 means the visible atoms must always form a tetrahedron.
misconception.M2: Ask which of the four tetrahedral domain positions contain nuclei at carbon and nitrogen.
misconception.M3: Keep electron-domain geometry (all domains) separate from molecular shape (bonded-atom positions).

items.independent_check: Carbon: 4 bonded positions + 0 lone pairs; nitrogen: 3 bonded positions + 1 lone pair. Both total 4 domains but their bonded-atom subsets differ.

items.verified_answer: Three sigma-bond directions and no lone pair give three local electron domains, so the introductory local model is sp2. Three sp2 hybrid orbitals provide the three coplanar sigma directions. The one remaining unhybridised p orbital is perpendicular to that plane and supplies the atomic orbital for the pi component. It is not a fourth electron-domain direction and is not one of the three sigma hybrids.
items.X: How to allocate one carbon's valence orbitals to three sigma directions plus one pi participation without reusing or double-counting an orbital.
items.Y: The authored anchor is the sp2 orbital inventory: three hybrids plus one unhybridised p orbital.
items.Z: Assign each of the three sigma directions to a distinct sp2 hybrid and reserve the unhybridised p orbital for pi overlap.
items.W: Complete a one-to-one orbital-job inventory showing 3 sp2 sigma orbitals + 1 p pi orbital and no duplicate assignment.
hints: Make an inventory with two columns: sigma-framework orbitals and pi-participating orbitals.
Three local domains call for three coplanar sp2 hybrid directions in the introductory model.
After assigning those three, exactly one carbon p orbital remains unhybridised; use it only for the pi job and check that no orbital appears twice.

representation.reason: An interactive staged orbital inventory is the most direct support for the no-double-counting representation demand.

misconception.M1: Count the pi bond as a fourth domain or reuse one sp2 hybrid orbital for both a sigma and pi component.
misconception.M2: Ask the learner to tick off each local carbon valence orbital exactly once against a bonding job.
misconception.M3: Hybridize three orbitals into the sp2 sigma set and keep the fourth p orbital separate for pi overlap; domain count and orbital inventory are related but not identical ledgers.

items.independent_check: The local valence-orbital inventory closes at four: three sp2 hybrids assigned to sigma directions and one unhybridised p assigned to pi participation.

items.verified_answer: The statement is false. CH4, NH3 and H2O each have four central electron domains and therefore tetrahedral electron-domain geometry in VSEPR. CH4 has 0 lone pairs, so four bonded atoms form a tetrahedral molecular shape; NH3 has 1 lone pair, so three bonded atoms form a trigonal-pyramidal shape; H2O has 2 lone pairs, so two bonded atoms form a bent shape. Electron-domain geometry includes lone pairs; molecular shape names the atom positions.
items.X: Whether tetrahedral electron-domain geometry logically entails tetrahedral molecular shape.
items.Y: The demonstrated four-domain rule plus the explicit distinction that molecular shape includes atom positions rather than lone-pair positions.
items.Z: Compare CH4, NH3 and H2O while holding four total domains fixed and varying lone-pair occupancy.
items.W: Reject the universal statement with NH3/H2O counterexamples and state the correct electron-domain-versus-molecular-shape warrant.
hints: Hold the total central domain count fixed at four for all three examples.
Now list how many of the four domain positions contain bonded atoms rather than lone pairs.
A molecular-shape name follows the atom positions only; use NH3 or H2O as the decisive counterexample.

representation.reason: A common four-domain scaffold with 0/1/2 lone-pair occupancy supports the counterexample and prevents conflating the two geometry names.

misconception.M1: Electron-domain geometry and molecular shape are interchangeable names whenever the domain geometry is tetrahedral.
misconception.M2: Ask the learner to count visible bonded atoms while separately retaining all four electron domains.
misconception.M3: Electron-domain geometry names all electron regions; molecular shape is the geometry of bonded atoms after lone-pair positions are omitted.

items.independent_check: All three examples total four electron domains, but their atom counts around the centre are 4, 3 and 2, producing tetrahedral, trigonal-pyramidal and bent molecular shapes respectively.
